Testimony of Mayor of the City of Portland, Mark Dion
Before
Committee on Housing and Economic Development
In Opposition to
LD 1179, An Act to Establish Minimum Safety Standards for Temporary Emergency Shelters
April 8, 2025
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and Members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development:
On behalf of the City of Portland, I write to express our opposition to LD 1179, An Act to Establish Minimum Safety Standards for Temporary Emergency Shelters.
Portland has long led the state in providing emergency shelter and wraparound services for individuals and families experiencing homelessness. We have done so not only to meet our obligations under the General Assistance statute, but because we believe in the fundamental value of ensuring that every Mainer has a safe place to sleep. As of 2024, Portland operates approximately 583 shelter beds across multiple facilities, including the Homeless Services Center, family shelter, and overflow sites for asylum seekers. This represents a substantial share of the state's total shelter capacity, which is estimated at around 1,170 beds statewide.
While we appreciate the intent behind LD 1179, to ensure basic safety standards for temporary emergency shelters, we cannot support this bill as written. It would create a new layer of state-mandated regulation over shelter operations without providing any corresponding funding or resources. In effect, it represents yet another unfunded mandate on the very municipalities that are already doing the most to meet this urgent and growing need.
This bill also raises serious home rule concerns. Local governments are best positioned to assess site-specific sheltering needs and respond quickly to emerging crises. Portland already has safety protocols in place, in close coordination with our fire department and code enforcement teams, to ensure that temporary emergency shelters meet appropriate health and safety standards. Adding a

new state regulatory structure could slow down our ability to act in real time--particularly during extreme weather or surges in need. Municipalities should retain flexibility and autonomy to operate shelters in a manner responsive to local conditions, capacity, and staffing. We urge the Committee to reject LD 1179. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Mark Dion Mayor City of Portland, Maine

Testimony ofRep. Poppy Arford in support of
LD 1179, "An Act to Establish Minimum Safety Standards for the Construction and Use of
Temporary Emergency Housing"
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development

Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and distinguished members of the Housing and Economic
Development Committee: My name is Poppy Arford, and I proudly represent State House
District 101s' business area, residential neighborhoods, farmland, coastal and river waters of Brunswick.
I offer this testimony in support of LD I179, "An Act to Establish Minimum Safety Standards
for the Construction and Use ofTe1npora1y Emergency Housing." As the sponsor, Rep. Macias, has described, this bill would provide municipalities with the guidance they need to safely locate temporary emergency housing for veterans within their borders. I agree wholeheartedly that we
must provide men and woman who have defended our country with the most basic necessity of
life: safe emergency housing when they find themselves unhoused and in need.

I respect and understand that this committee hears a comprehensive mix of bills to remedy the
harms resulting from Maine's ongoing housing crisis. My understanding is also that the type of emergency housing we are discussing is ALREADY an available remedy, already easing the
housing crisis burden for Maine veterans and their families. At this time, 45 total units exist, 35
are deployed statewide, 6 more are under construction, and 12 additional units are on order. We
need one in Brunswick, yet to date, the lack of State rules and guidance on acceptable, safe heating units has prevented us from making final arrangements to host one.
In support of adequate units and locations statewide, I join with Rep. Macias in asking that LD 1179 receive an OTP vote. I also urge the Commissioner of Public Safety to move swiftly once LD 1179 becomes law to issue interim guidance while permanent rules are developed, so that
organizations like Boothbay V.E.T.S. may continue their undeniably good Work to house Maine
veterans.

In closing, I thank you for your time and consideration of my testimony.

Testimony of Rep. Rafael Macias introducing
LD 1179, An Act to Establish Minimum Safety Standards for the Construction and
Use. of Temporary Emergency Shelters
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development

Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Housing and Economic Development, my name is Rafael Macias, and I represent House District 51,
which includes part of Topsham. I am here today to introduce LD 1179, An Act to Establish Minimum
Safety Standards for the Construction and Use of Temporary Emergency Shelters.
I gratefully authored and sponsored LD 1179, a bill that speaks to both our values and our
responsibilities, especially to those who have worn the uniform and now find themselves without shelter.

This bill establishes minimum safety standards for temporary emergency shelters, like the mobile units
being built in Boothbay Harbor by an organization called Boothbay V.E.T.S.----Veterans Emergency Temporary Shelter. These are compact, insulated shelters on wheels. They come with electricity, heat, a
portable toilet, a refrigerator, and even a microwave. And they're being placed where they're most
welcome, on veterans` organizations grounds like the American Legions around the state, for veterans
who would otherwise be on the street.

LD 1179 is not about red tape. It's about life and safety.
We have a duty to ensure that these shelters, while temporary, meet basic standards: safe heating
systems, proper ventilation, and a way out in an emergency beyond just the front door. These are not luxury additions. They're the difference between a warm, survivable winter night and a fire hazard,
between a lifeline and a liability.

But I also want to be clear about what this bill is not. It is not a tool for shutting down community-based
responses to homelessness. It is not a license for municipalities to say "no" to emergency housing efforts
out of fear or misunderstanding. In fact, it's the opposite. By providing clear, reasonable safety standards, We are giving local governments and nonprofits the confidence to say "yes."

Still, I recognize the concern that regulation, however well-intended, can sometimes have unintended
consequences. That's why I support adding flexibility in implementation. I would like the rulemaking
process to include a grace period, technical assistance, and most importantly--a clear path for

District 51: Part of Topsham

community groups to come into compliance without being punished for acting in good faith to help
others.

I also urge that the Commissioner of Public Safety move swiftly to issue interim guidance while
permanent rules are developed, so that organizations like Boothbay V.E.T.S. aren't left in limbo.

This is a Maine solution to a national crisis. And it honors our veterans, our volunteers, and our values

Let's pass LD 1179 and build safety into our compassion.

.

Thank you.

District 51: Part of Topsham

LD 1179 - LD 1179 An Act to Establish Minimum Safety Standards for the Construction and Use of
Temporary Emergency Shelters
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Housing and Economic Development:
Committee, my name is Shawn Esler, and it is a privilege to serve as the State Fire Marshal.
I write neither for nor against LD ll79.
The Office of State Fire Marshal has adopted by statue National Fire Protection Codes and Intemational Building Codes that guide us for shelters either permanent or temporary on how they are prepared for occupancy. Since the beginning of Covid in 2019, our office has worked with several municipalities in the
State for emergency shelters. We hope to continue those strong relationships.
The building and fire codes approach construction in two ways: 1) Prescriptive codes 2) Performance
based codes.
Prescriptive codes specify exact materials, methods, and designs to achieve an outcome.
Performance based codes focus on desired outcomes allowing for flexibility in achieving those goals.
LD 1179 as written would require prescriptive fire codes. We feel it is best in striving for performance-
based codes that focus on the desired outcome rather than specifying the exact means to achieve it. This
gives the FMO and local jurisdictions more discretion for compliance in trying times where an emergency
shelter may be needed, especially in cases where occupancy is less than 24 hours.
LD 1179 as written requests fire code standards for the design and construction of temporary emergency
shelters, including ventilation requirements, electrical safety and emergency exits. If the Fire Marshal
Office is to complete this task with the intent as written in this legislation, we will require hiring or
contracting with a qualified engineer or architect to achieve the rewriting of rules. Writing prescriptive
fire code is beyond the expertise of the FMO.
The Fire Marshal's Office will assist in any work session regarding fire codes and emergency shelters. It is our recommendation to soften the language to allow performance-based codes to guide emergency
sheltering.
